To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The use of resistance testing in low-income settings is not cost-effective and should be discontinued.

(i) resistance testing in low-resource settings is not a cost-effective strategy to improve second-line treatment outcomes; (ii) resistance testing in resource-limited settings should be restricted to those with a history of virological failure; and (iii) resistance testing should only be performed in settings where the cost of resistance testing is less than the cost of second-line treatment.

(i) in the setting of a high prevalence of transmitted drug resistance, the use of second-line regimens that do not contain a pharmacologically enhanced PI is not associated with a higher rate of virological failure, and (ii) in the setting with a low prevalence of transmitted drug, the use of a PI-sparing second-line regimen is not associated with higher rates of virological or clinical failure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of HIV drug resistance on second-line therapy in low and middle income countries.
the development of a mathematical model to investigate the impact of drug resistance on the effectiveness of antiretrovival treatment.
the use of antiretrovirus (ARV) therapy for HIV/AIDS in low and middle-income (LMIC) countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of resistance testing for guiding ART in resource-limited settings is not recommended at present, and that further research is urgently needed.
the current evidence does not support the routine use of resistance testing for the selection of second-line therapy in low- and middle-income settings.
the current evidence does not support the use of resistance testing for treatment decisions in resource-poor settings, but that further research is needed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
resistance testing may not always be the best use of resources in a low-income setting.
the use of resistance testing to guide ART switching is unlikely to be cost-effective in most resource-constrained settings.
the current approach of testing for drug resistance before switching to second-line treatment is not cost-effective and may not be the best use of resources.

resistance testing may not always be the best use of resources in low-income settings.
the WHO recommendation for second-line therapy is still appropriate in the absence of resistance testing.
